title: Clay tokens and sealed envelopes (bullae) of the Late Uruk period
summary: In the Late Uruk period, accountants at Susa and in southern Mesopotamia sealed clay tokens, standing for goods such as grain and animals, inside hollow clay balls called bullae or envelopes. Impressing the tokens on the outside let the contents be checked unbroken, an accounting step scholars link to the first writing.

uncertainty.note: The University of Texas pages give c. 3300 BC for the Susa envelope and 3350–3100 BC for the first impressed texts; the BnF dates a sealed Susa bulla c. 3300 BC; the Louvre catalogue gives c. 3500–2900 BC (Proto-urban) for its SB 1932 bulla.

related.because: In Schmandt-Besserat's account, impressing tokens on envelopes and then on clay tablets led to the first written signs.

reviewer_note: Dates differ: Schmandt-Besserat and the BnF say c. 3300 BC; the Louvre catalogue gives a wider range and uses "Proto-urbain", not "Late Uruk". The "envelope as step to writing" reading is Schmandt-Besserat's theory and is debated; I did not open critiques. Pin is modern Shush beside the Susa ruins.

beats.caption: Around 3300 BCE tokens for grain and flocks were enclosed in a hollow clay envelope at Susa.
Their shapes were pressed into the outer surface so the contents could be checked without breaking the envelope.
Schmandt-Besserat argues the flattened impressions became signs on solid clay tablets, an early step toward writing.
